name: Abijah
title: Judas second king after the division of the kingdom
summary: Abijah, who is called Abijam in the Books of Kings, took over the kingship in Judah after his father Rehoboam and ruled the kingdom for about three years. He is above all known for the decisive battle against Jeroboam, king of the northern kingdom, where he, with a numerically inferior army, called upon the Lord's intervention and won a crushing victory. Before the fight, from Mount Zemaraim, he delivered a striking speech in which he asserted the Davidic dynasty's rightful claim over all Israel and defended the lawful temple service in Jerusalem against Jeroboam's idolatry with golden calves. The biblical sources give a tension-filled portrait: the Books of Kings judge him as unfaithful to the Lord and like his father in sin, while the Books of Chronicles highlight his rhetorical defense of true worship and the divine victory. This duality illustrates a central biblical theme—that God's faithfulness to the covenant with David stands regardless of the individual king's moral conduct. Abijah is also mentioned as a link in the messianic lineage from David to Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew.

keyEvents.title: Abijah becomes king over Judah
keyEvents.description: After the death of his father Rehoboam, Abijah was installed as the second king of Judah in Jerusalem and reigned for three years.

keyEvents.title: War against Jeroboam
keyEvents.description: Abijah waged a great war against Jeroboam of Israel with an army of 400,000 men against Jeroboam's 800,000.

keyEvents.title: Abijah's Speech on Mount Zemaraim
keyEvents.description: Before the battle, Abijah delivered a powerful speech defending the rightful claim of David's dynasty to the throne and the legitimate worship in the temple in Jerusalem, while accusing Jeroboam of abandoning the Lord and introducing idolatry with golden calves.

keyEvents.title: God's Victory over Jeroboam
keyEvents.description: Despite being greatly outnumbered, Abijah and Judah cried out to the Lord, and the priests blew trumpets. God struck down Jeroboam, and Israel suffered a massive defeat.

keyEvents.title: Abijah's Large Family
keyEvents.description: Abijah strengthened the royal house through a deliberate dynastic policy. He took fourteen wives and fathered twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters.

keyEvents.title: The Assessment of Abijah's Reign
keyEvents.description: In the Books of Kings, Abijah is described as one who walked in all the sins his father had committed, and his heart was not fully devoted to the Lord as David's heart had been. Nevertheless, God allowed his line to continue for David's sake.

keyEvents.title: Abijah's Death and Asa's Accession
keyEvents.description: After three years of reign, Abijah died and was buried in the City of David. His son Asa became king after him.

keyEvents.title: Abijah in Jesus' Genealogy
keyEvents.description: Abijah is mentioned in the genealogy in the Gospel of Matthew as a link in the messianic line from Abraham through David to Jesus Christ.

versions.summary: Abijah (also known as Abijam) was the son of Rehoboam and the second king of the southern kingdom of Judah after the division of Israel. He reigned for three years and waged war against Jeroboam of Israel. Although he did not follow the Lord wholeheartedly, God granted him victory because of the covenant with David.

versions.summary:
Abijah (also known as Abijam) was the son of Rehoboam and the second king in the southern kingdom of Judah after the division of Israel.  
He reigned for three years and led a major war against Jeroboam of Israel.  
The books of Kings evaluate him negatively, stating that his heart was not fully devoted to the Lord, while the books of Chronicles highlight his defense of legitimate worship in Jerusalem and the great victory God gave him over Jeroboam.  
Despite his moral weaknesses, God upheld David’s dynasty because of the covenant with David.  
Abijah is also mentioned in Jesus’ genealogy.

versions.summary: Abijah, also called Abijam, succeeded his father Rehoboam as king of Judah and reigned for about three years. He is best known for the dramatic confrontation with Jeroboam, king of the northern kingdom, where from Mount Zemaraim he delivered a powerful speech defending the rightful claim of David's dynasty and true worship at the temple in Jerusalem. Despite having a numerically inferior army, Judah won an overwhelming victory attributed to God's intervention. The Bible presents a complex picture of Abijah: the Books of Kings describe him as unfaithful to the Lord, while the Books of Chronicles highlight his defense of proper worship. God's faithfulness to the Davidic covenant ensured the dynasty's continuation even through a morally ambiguous king. Abijah is also included in the messianic genealogy in the Gospel of Matthew.

footnotes.text: The name 'Abijah' (Hebrew: אֲבִיָּה, Aviyyah) means 'my father is Yahweh' or 'Yahweh is father'. In 1 Kings, the form 'Abijam' (אֲבִיָּם) is used, which may mean 'father of the sea' or be a variant of the same name. The variation in names may stem from different textual traditions, and some scholars have suggested that 'Abijam' was a deliberate change to avoid associating the divine name Yahweh with a negative king.

The portrayal of Abijah differs markedly between 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles. The book of Kings paints a negative picture where his heart was not fully with the Lord (1 Kgs 15:3), while Chronicles highlights his faithful speech and the great victory God gave him over Jeroboam (2 Chr 13). This difference reflects the two books' distinct theological perspectives: Chronicles emphasizes legitimate temple service in Jerusalem and positive traits of the kings of Judah, whereas Kings evaluates more strictly based on faithfulness to the Lord.

Abijah's mother is called 'Maacah, daughter of Absalom' in 1 Kings 15:2, but 'Micaiah, daughter of Uriel from Gibeah' in 2 Chronicles 13:2. This apparent contradiction can be explained by the fact that 'daughter' in Hebrew (bat) can also mean 'granddaughter', that Maacah and Micaiah may be two forms of the same name, or that Absalom and Uriel refer to different generations. Some scholars believe Maacah was Absalom's granddaughter through Tamar (cf. 2 Samuel 14:27).

The casualty figure of 500,000 fallen Israelites (2 Chronicles 13:17) is debated among scholars. The Hebrew word 'elef' (אֶלֶף) can mean both 'thousand' and 'military unit' or 'clan', which may imply that the numbers should be understood as military units rather than individuals. Regardless of interpretation, the narrative point is that Judah achieved an overwhelming and unexpected victory.

Mount Zemaraim, where Abijah delivered his speech (2 Chronicles 13:4), is likely connected to the city of Zemaraim mentioned in Joshua 18:22 in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. Its location in the border region between Judah and Israel underscores the geopolitical context of the conflict between the two kingdoms.

In Matthew's genealogy (Matthew 1:7), Abijah (Greek: Ἀβιά) is mentioned as a link in the lineage from Abraham to Jesus. This places him within the messianic line and emphasizes that God's promises to David were fulfilled through this dynastic line, despite the moral weaknesses of individual kings.

According to 2 Chronicles 13:21, Abijah had fourteen wives, twenty-two sons, and sixteen daughters. This large number of wives and children reflects a deliberate dynastic policy, possibly inspired by his father's example (cf. 2 Chronicles 11:21), and shows a strategy for consolidating power despite the short reign.

Rabbinic tradition has discussed Abijah's character in light of the conflicting biblical accounts. Some rabbis believed that his speech against Jeroboam demonstrated genuine piety, while others viewed it as opportunistic rhetoric from a king who himself did not follow the Lord wholeheartedly. The Talmud (Sotah 10a) suggests that his positive actions were motivated by politics rather than faith.
